DE FACTO PARENT STATUS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · stepparent

DE FACTO PARENT STATUS REQUEST — INFORMATION AND DECLARATION
I, Jordan Lee, am not Casey Lee's legal or biological parent. My relationship to Casey Lee, a minor born January 1, 2018, is: stepparent. This information sheet provides background information about California's de facto parent doctrine -- a status a juvenile court may recognize, on a sufficient showing, for a person who has assumed a day-to-day parental role in a child's life -- for use alongside an actual application for de facto parent status in a pending Welfare and Institutions Code section 300 juvenile dependency proceeding concerning Casey Lee, in the San Francisco County Superior Court (juvenile division) or other court of competent jurisdiction. This information sheet is not itself an application for de facto parent status, and it is not a court filing; signing it does not grant Jordan Lee de facto parent status, custody, or visitation of Casey Lee. Casey Lee's legal parent(s) of record, so far as known, are Taylor Morgan and Riley Chen, where applicable. Only a court's own finding, on a sufficient showing, that Jordan Lee has assumed the day-to-day role of parent to Casey Lee can grant de facto parent status, and, as this document's other clauses describe, that status itself does not make Jordan Lee Casey Lee's legal parent or guardian and does not itself grant custody or visitation.

WHAT "DE FACTO PARENT" STATUS MEANS, AND THE JUVENILE-DEPENDENCY CONTEXT IN WHICH THE TERM IS DEFINED — CALIFORNIA RULES OF COURT, RULE 5.502(10)
California Rules of Court, rule 5.502(10) defines the term for use throughout the state's juvenile court rules: "'De facto parent' means a person who has been found by the court to have assumed, on a day-to-day basis, the role of parent, fulfilling both the child's physical and psychological needs for care and affection, and who has assumed that role for a substantial period." This is a status a court finds to exist on a sufficient showing -- it does not arise automatically merely from providing care, and, as this document's other clauses describe, it is not the same as being Casey Lee's legal parent. Rule 5.502's own preamble lists the statutory provisions its definitions serve, and every one of them is a Welfare and Institutions Code section (for example, sections 300, 303, 319, 361, and 361.5(a)(3)) or a related federal statute -- none is a Family Code section. That confirms that "de facto parent," as this rule defines and uses it, is a term of art within California's juvenile dependency court system, not within the general Family Code custody and visitation framework addressed in this corpus's separate Third-Party (Nonparent) Custody and Visitation document.

  — Cal. Rules of Court, rule 5.502(10) (Judicial Council of California, courts.ca.gov text), Cal. Rules of Court, rule 5.502(10) (https://courts.ca.gov/cms/rules/index/five/rule5_502)
  "Definitions (§§ 202(e), 303, 319, 361, 361.5(a)(3), 450, 628.1, 636, 726, 727.3(c)(2), 727.4(d), 4512(j), 4701.6(b), 11400(v), 11400(y), 16501(f)(16); 20 U.S.C. § 1415; 25 U.S.C. § 1903(2))"
  — Cal. Rules of Court, rule 5.502, definitions preamble (Judicial Council of California, courts.ca.gov text), Cal. Rules of Court, rule 5.502 (preamble) (https://courts.ca.gov/cms/rules/index/five/rule5_502)

This clause cites two parts of the same rule -- the definitions preamble and subdivision (10) -- so this is not independent corroboration from two separate sources, only two parts of one source; that is disclosed here rather than presented as independent confirmation. This corrects an assumption in the research request that prompted this document: California Family Code sections 3040 and 7601 were independently fetched and re-fetched (courts.ca.gov and leginfo.legislature.ca.gov are treated separately for this purpose) and, as of the dates checked, neither section's text uses the phrase "de facto parent" anywhere -- the corpus's existing Third-Party (Nonparent) Custody and Visitation document's coverage of Family Code section 3040(a)(3)'s "any other person" custody-preference language and section 3100(a)'s "any other person having an interest in the welfare of the child" visitation language remains accurate on its own terms, but neither provision is, on its face, the statutory home of the de facto parent doctrine. This clause does not resolve whether a party to a Family Code custody or visitation proceeding could, as a factual matter, also independently qualify for the very different Family Code pathways described in that companion document; it addresses only the Rules of Court' own definition and its juvenile-dependency statutory anchoring.

THE STANDING AND THE THREE SPECIFIC RIGHTS DE FACTO PARENT STATUS CONFERS — CALIFORNIA RULES OF COURT, RULE 5.534(A)
California Rules of Court, rule 5.534(a) states what recognition as a de facto parent actually does for a person in a dependency case: "On a sufficient showing, the court may recognize the child's present or previous custodian as a de facto parent and grant him or her standing to participate as a party in the dispositional hearing and any hearing thereafter at which the status of the dependent child is at issue." The rule then lists exactly what that standing includes: "The de facto parent may: (1) Be present at the hearing; (2) Be represented by retained counsel or, at the discretion of the court, by appointed counsel; and (3) Present evidence." Recognition is discretionary ("the court may recognize"), conditioned on "a sufficient showing," and, by the rule's own terms, tied to the dispositional hearing and later hearings concerning Casey Lee's status as a dependent -- not to every stage of a case.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]

The de facto parent may: (1) Be present at the hearing; (2) Be represented by retained counsel or, at the discretion of the court, by appointed counsel; and (3) Present evidence."
  — Cal. Rules of Court, rule 5.534(a) (Judicial Council of California, courts.ca.gov text), Cal. Rules of Court, rule 5.534(a) (https://courts.ca.gov/cms/rules/index/five/rule5_534)

This clause quotes a single subdivision, rule 5.534(a); the rule's separate subdivision (b), which gives a relative of the child a narrower right (to be present and address the court, without the retained- or appointed-counsel right this subdivision gives a de facto parent), was not independently quoted here. The rule does not itself define "a sufficient showing" -- this document's companion clause on In re B.G. (1974) 11 Cal.3d 679 addresses the standard California's courts have used for that showing, but this clause does not resolve how that standard applies to any specific applicant's facts. This clause also does not address whether, or how, a person recognized as a de facto parent may participate at the separate jurisdictional hearing (the hearing at which the truth of the allegations that brought the case into dependency court is decided, as distinct from the dispositional hearing this rule's text names) -- that question was not independently researched for this document. Nothing in this rule's text grants a de facto parent custody, visitation, reunification services, or any right beyond the three this subdivision lists.

ORIGIN OF THE DOCTRINE AND THE STANDARD FOR DETERMINING WHO QUALIFIES — IN RE B.G. (1974) 11 CAL.3D 679
California's de facto parent doctrine originated in the California Supreme Court's 1974 decision In re B.G., which coined the term: "We use the term 'de facto parent' to refer to that person who, on a day-to-day basis, assumes the role of parent, seeking to fulfill both the child's physical needs and his psychological need for affection and care." The court held that a person meeting that description "should be permitted to appear as parties in juvenile court proceedings," not merely as a friend of the court: "Their standing should not depend upon the filing of a petition for guardianship, although the filing of such petition may aid in attesting to their interest in the custody of the child; nor should their participation be restricted to the limited role of an amicus curiae; they should be permitted to appear as parties to assert and protect their own interest in the companionship, care, custody and management of the child." On the standard for qualifying, the court did not set out a rigid checklist: "We anticipate that juvenile courts will experience little difficulty in determining whether a person is a de facto parent for purposes of standing to appear in a juvenile court custody proceeding. The simple fact that a person cares enough to seek and undertake to participate goes far to suggest that the court would profit by hearing his views as to the child's best interests; if the participant lacks a close relationship with the child, that fact will undoubtedly emerge during the proceedings."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]

Their standing should not depend upon the filing of a petition for guardianship, although the filing of such petition may aid in attesting to their interest in the custody of the child; nor should their participation be restricted to the limited role of an amicus curiae; they should be permitted to appear as parties to assert and protect their own interest in the companionship, care, custody and management of the child."
  — In re B.G. (1974) 11 Cal.3d 679, 692-693 (California Supreme Court), 11 Cal.3d 679, 692-693 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1163726/in-re-bg/)
  "We anticipate that juvenile courts will experience little difficulty in determining whether a person is a de facto parent for purposes of standing to appear in a juvenile court custody proceeding. The simple fact that a person cares enough to seek and undertake to participate goes far to suggest that the court would profit by hearing his views as to the child's best interests; if the participant lacks a close relationship with the child, that fact will undoubtedly emerge during the proceedings."
  — In re B.G. (1974) 11 Cal.3d 679, 693, fn. 18 (California Supreme Court), 11 Cal.3d 679, 693, fn. 18 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1163726/in-re-bg/)

This 1974 decision predates the current numbering of the California Rules of Court; this document's companion clauses cite the doctrine's present codification at rule 5.502(10) and rule 5.534(a), but this document does not independently trace the renumbering history between 1974 and today. DE FACTO PARENT STATUS IS NOT LEGAL PARENTAGE OR GUARDIANSHIP, AND DOES NOT CARRY ALL OF A LEGAL PARENT'S RIGHTS — IN RE B.G., FN. 21, AND IN RE KIESHIA E.
In re B.G. itself limited what the de facto parent status it created actually means: "We do not hold that a de facto parent is a 'parent' or 'guardian' as those terms are used in the Juvenile Court Law, nor do we express a position whether constitutional principles of due process or equal protection may require that a de facto parent, in some instances, receive rights of notice, hearing, or counsel afforded natural parents or guardians under that law." Nearly twenty years later, the California Supreme Court in In re Kieshia E. restated that limit and confirmed it remained the law: "In re B.G., supra, expressly declined to hold that nonparents who assume a parental role thereby become 'parents' or 'guardians,' with all the rights such a status implies." The Kieshia E. court added that Courts of Appeal had likewise held that de facto parents "are not equated with ... parents or guardians for purposes of dependency proceedings and standing to participate does not give them all of the rights and preferences accorded [parents or guardians]." In practical terms, and read together with this document's companion clause on rule 5.534(a): de facto parent status gives Jordan Lee the right to be present, to be represented by counsel, and to present evidence at the specified hearings concerning Casey Lee -- it does not, by itself, make Jordan Lee Casey Lee's legal parent or guardian, and it does not itself grant custody, visitation, or the reunification services or other statutory entitlements the Juvenile Court Law affords a legal parent or guardian.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "We do not hold that a de facto parent is a "parent" or "guardian" as those terms are used in the Juvenile Court Law, nor do we express a position whether constitutional principles of due process or equal protection may require that a de facto parent, in some instances, receive rights of notice, hearing, or counsel afforded natural parents or guardians under that law."
  — In re B.G. (1974) 11 Cal.3d 679, 693, fn. 21 (California Supreme Court), 11 Cal.3d 679, 693, fn. 21 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1163726/in-re-bg/)
  "expressly declined to hold that nonparents who assume a parental role thereby become "parents" or "guardians," with all the rights such a status implies."
  — In re Kieshia E. (1993) 6 Cal.4th 68, 77 (California Supreme Court), 6 Cal.4th 68, 77 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2613175/in-re-kieshia-e/)
  "Subsequent Court of Appeal decisions have confirmed that even those who attain the status of de facto parenthood "are not equated with ... parents or guardians for purposes of dependency proceedings and standing to participate does not give them all of the rights and preferences accorded [parents or guardians]. [Citations.]....""
  — In re Kieshia E. (1993) 6 Cal.4th 68, 77 (California Supreme Court), 6 Cal.4th 68, 77 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2613175/in-re-kieshia-e/)
  Known gap: The Kieshia E. quotations were read from two independently formatted CourtListener source records for the same opinion -- one captioned "In re Kieshia E." (opinion id 2613175) and one captioned "San Diego County Department of Social Services v. Williams" (opinion id 5452096), both carrying the identical official citation, 6 Cal.4th 68, 859 P.2d 1290, 23 Cal.Rptr.2d 775 -- and the quoted passages were confirmed to match across both records. That said, this clause's two case-law citations are not fully independent of each other in substance: Kieshia E.'s own quoted passage is expressly restating and quoting In re B.G.'s footnote 21, and, in turn, quoting a Court of Appeal decision, In re Rachael C. (1991) 235 Cal.App.3d 1445, 1452, that this document does not independently verify -- so this clause offers one line of authority (B.G., reaffirmed and extended by Kieshia E.), not two unrelated ones. Separately, Kieshia E.'s actual holding was narrower and more fact-specific than the general limitation quoted here: the court held that an adult who committed the sexual or other serious physical abuse that caused a child to become a juvenile court dependent cannot attain or retain de facto parent status as to that child. That specific holding is noted here for context but is not itself summarized or relied on as this clause's point; this clause's point is only the general, unqualified proposition -- true independent of Kieshia E.'s facts -- that de facto parent status is not legal parentage or guardianship and does not carry all of a legal parent's rights. This clause does not address, and this document does not independently research, how a legal parent's rights and entitlements under the Juvenile Court Law compare item-by-item to a de facto parent's.
